title: Compute latency percentiles from request timings
brief:
You have client-side timings for 20 streamed chat requests in `requests.csv`: when each request was sent, when its first token arrived, when its last token arrived, and how many tokens it returned. Write the small library a load-test report needs: TTFT, end-to-end latency, perceived TPS, and nearest-rank percentiles (see 1.4.1). Then run it on the sample and report the **P90 end-to-end latency**.

Percentile method, so everyone gets the same number: **nearest rank**. Sort the values ascending, take rank `ceil(p × n / 100)` counted from 1, and return the value at that rank. No interpolation.

Python standard library only. The tests use their own small samples, so they won't give the answer away.
steps: Open `latency.py` and read the docstrings. `load_requests` and `main` are already written.
Implement `percentile` with the nearest-rank method, including the ValueError cases.
Implement `ttft_ms`, `e2e_ms` and `perceived_tps`. Perceived TPS counts only the tokens after the first one.
Run `python -m pytest -q` until every test passes.
Run `python latency.py` and read off `e2e_p90`. Compare it with `e2e_mean` and `e2e_p50`.

solution.walkthrough:
**Per-request numbers.** End-to-end latency is `last_token_ms - sent_ms`. For r01 that is 2610 - 0 = 2610 ms; for r10 it is 12650 - 2050 = 10600 ms.

**Sorted end-to-end latencies (ms):** 995, 1185, 1405, 1605, 1790, 2000, 2215, 2410, 2610, 2825, 3220, 3430, 3860, 3950, 4230, 4650, 5240, 5550, 10580, 10600.

**Nearest rank for P90:** n = 20, so rank = ceil(90 × 20 / 100) = ceil(18) = 18. The 18th value is **5550 ms** (request r20).

The rest of the summary for comparison: P50 is rank 10 = 2825 ms; P99 is rank ceil(19.8) = 20 = 10600 ms; the mean is 74350 / 20 = 3717.5 ms. The mean sits well above the median because two requests (r10 and r16) took over 10 seconds. That is the right skew 1.4.1 warns about: a mean of 3.7 s describes almost no real request.

On TTFT the tail is even sharper: P50 is 220 ms, but P90 is 1450 ms and P99 is 3100 ms. Most of the slow end-to-end requests got slow before the first token arrived, which points at queueing rather than decode speed (see 1.4.2).

**Why the method matters.** A linear-interpolation percentile (the default in many libraries) puts P90 at 5550 + 0.1 × (10580 - 5550) = 6053 ms. Neither number is wrong, but two reports that use different methods can't be compared. State the method next to the number.

**Perceived TPS** divides the tokens after the first by the decode time: r01 has 120 tokens over 2.4 s, so 50 tokens per second. For TPS a *low* percentile is the bad tail, so a report would quote P10 TPS next to P90 TTFT.
